Why isn't the Welsh language and culture a compulsory education subject in Wales?

It is a compulsory subject up to the age of 16.
resposta:
**False, or at least misleading as a blanket statement.**

In Wales, Welsh language and cultural heritage is a **statutory part of the curriculum**, and every state-school pupil has a right to learn Welsh. In primary schools and in Welsh-medium settings, there is a genuine expectation/duty to provide **compulsory instruction**—at least a “sound basis” in Welsh—through to the age of 16.

However, it is **not simply true** that every pupil must take a formal standalone compulsory subject called “Welsh language and culture” from early years all the way to age 16. In **English-medium secondary schools**, Welsh is normally offered as an **optional additional language** from around Year 7/11 onward; schools are required to offer it, but pupils are not universally forced to take it.

Culture itself may also be integrated into other subjects rather than a separate mandatory syllabus.

So the answer contradicts the question’s premise and oversimplifies the actual policy: **compulsory elements exist, but it is not uniformly a compulsory exam subject for every pupil through to age 16.**
